Anwar said this at the Sentuhan Kasih Madani Programme and launch of the National Cost of Living Action Plan 2030 (NCLAP30) at the Hang Jebat Sports Complex here yesterday. Also present was Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Minister Datuk Armizan Mohd Ali.
The prime minister said international investor confidence in Malaysia must be sustained through political stability, firm leadership, and a conducive economic climate.
Anwar cited peace and harmony among the country's multiracial and multireligious communities as a key strength that must be leveraged to attract foreign capital.
"If people don't have confidence in this government, and if the leadership is constantly quarrelling, investors will not be interested in coming here," he said.
Anwar said Malaysia must continue strengthening its capabilities in emerging technologies, particularly AI, digitalisation, and semiconductors, to ensure sustainable economic growth.
He said workforce training and skills development are vital to help Malaysia move beyond back-end technology activities into higher-value middle- and front-end segments.
He said the success in attracting investments must ultimately translate into tangible benefits for the people, including higher living standards and quality jobs.
5d46fae5d0287aab: BAGAN DATUK, Oct 25 — Malaysia remains committed to its offer of assistance to Indonesia to address the transboundary haze affecting the country, said Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi.
He said the commitment had been discussed at the Cabinet meeting last Friday to ensure that appropriate measures could be coordinated for the benefit of both countries.

Ahmad Zahid said the Indonesian government had deployed more than 16,000 personnel along with various aircraft and firefighting helicopters, but aerial operations were facing challenges due to poor visibility. There was also a lack of cloud formations suitable for cloud-seeding operations.

“So, we sympathise with their situation. However, we still hope that this problem can be resolved because it is causing neighbouring countries, particularly Malaysia, to suffer the adverse effects of the haze on health, especially among those with conditions related to allergies caused by the haze,” he said.
He told reporters this after officiating at the Bagan Datuk 2026 Sultan Nazrin Shah Bridge Run here today.
Ahmad Zahid said bilateral communication had already been initiated at the highest level with the Indonesian government leadership to discuss the current situation.
On today’s running event, he said it had attracted 1,700 local and international participants, including from Australia, Indonesia, Singapore, France, India, Nepal and Thailand.
“It is better (organised) this year, but as was the case last year, heavy rain fell right up until now.
“Next year, we will upgrade it to a full marathon. Hopefully, more people will take part, and we pray that there will be no rain at that time,” he said.

The event featured three categories, with the 5km run recording the highest participation of 759 runners (44.6 per cent), followed by the 21km category with 575 participants (33.8 per cent) and the 10km category with 366 participants (21.5 per cent). — Bernama
549148b11ff25462: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 25 — With lunchtime approaching, Gerai Masakan Panas Che Daud in Taman Sri Rampai would normally be preparing for the midday crowd. But at 11.40am, stall owner Che Daud Che Isa had just one customer to attend to.
The 59-year-old said business had slowed since the haze began, with some customers choosing to pack their food and eat at home rather than sit down at his stall.
He estimated that customer numbers had fallen by about half, as worsening air quality appeared to discourage people from eating out.
“My stall is facing some problems now. Perhaps it is because of the haze and people are afraid to come out, so the number of customers has decreased.
“Some customers are also opting for takeaway. They do not want to eat at the stall and would rather take the food home. But even then, the numbers are not as high as before,” he told Malay Mail.

Che Daud’s experience reflects the challenges faced by eateries as the haze continues to affect air quality across the Klang Valley, with restaurant operators reporting fewer dine-in customers, falling sales and changes in dining habits.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Che Daud Che Isa, 59, said the ongoing haze has affected business at his food stall in Taman Sri Rampai, Kuala Lumpur, with customer numbers down by about half. — Picture by Muhammad Yusry
Despite the drop in foot traffic, some eateries continue to draw customers, although their regulars are increasingly opting for takeaway.

A restaurant worker about 200 metres from Che Daud’s stall, who asked not to be named, said those still dining in were often motorists who stopped for a meal while waiting for their cars to be serviced at nearby workshops.
At Warung Paman Sol restaurant in Taman Keramat, near the Jelatek LRT station, owner Solihin Faeez Mohd Shukri, 32, said daily income had fallen by between 20 and 25 per cent since the haze began.

While customers had not directly blamed the haze for staying away, he noticed that families who would normally dine in with their young children were increasingly sending one person to collect takeaway orders instead.
“There has definitely been a change in customer traffic,” he said, adding that takeaway and delivery orders had increased, although not significantly.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Solihin Faeez Mohd Shukri, 32, said he noticed that families who would normally dine in with their young children were increasingly sending one person to collect takeaway orders instead. — Picture by Muhammad Yusry
Solihin said he was keeping the restaurant’s operating arrangements unchanged for now, hoping the situation would improve soon.
But he was concerned that prolonged haze could have longer-term consequences for the restaurant business, as customers might become accustomed to ordering food for delivery rather than dining out.
“If it continues, I am worried that customer habits may change. Customers might become accustomed to using food delivery services and stop coming to restaurants to dine in,” he said.

In Shah Alam, the impact has also been felt at Miscusi Express in Seksyen 9, where Amir Habibur Rahman, 32, said sales had dropped by about 35 per cent in the past week compared with their usual level.
Amir said sales were initially largely unchanged, but the decline became more apparent about a week after the haze began.
He said fewer customers were coming in to eat, while those who did visit tended to look for indoor seating, an option his open-air establishment could not readily provide.
“There are also fewer people walking past the shop than usual,” he noted.
Although takeaway and delivery orders had remained steady, the loss of walk-in customers had affected overall sales.
Amir said he had no plans to change the shop’s operating hours, from noon to 10pm, as sales were usually strongest around lunchtime and in the afternoon.
Instead, the business was continuing to operate as usual while providing free face masks to customers who needed them.
The open-air setting had also meant more dust than usual, requiring the shop to be cleaned more frequently.
Amir was particularly concerned about the possibility of the haze dragging on for months, saying prolonged exposure could affect the health of both customers and workers.
“My hope is that the haze will not persist for too long, as some have predicted it could last until February next year.
“A lot of things have already been affected, and if the situation continues to threaten the health of our customers and employees, we may not be able to sustain the business," he said.

Malaysian Meteorological Department (MetMalaysia) director-general Mohd Hisham Mohd Anip previously told Malay Mail that the haze was expected to gradually subside next week following an anticipated change in wind direction.
During the North-east Monsoon, stronger north-easterly winds and more widespread rainfall were expected to help improve air quality, he said.
be0537bc06b21bba: KUALA LUMPUR: Local creative players are set for a major boost as the National Film Development Corporation Malaysia (Finas) opens applications for its RM15 million Creative Content Fund (DKK) starting Nov 16.

Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said the financial boost would help local talent collaborate internationally, nurture new creators, and produce fresh content for the fast-changing digital market.

The funding covers six main categories: the International Co-Production Fund (Feature Film or Animated Feature), the First Time Amateur Filmmaker (FAME) Fund, the Super Telefilm TV Programme Co-Production Fund, the Broadcaster/OTT Platform Micro Drama Co-Production Fund, the Veteran Artist Super Telefilm (STAR) Fund, and the National Public Service Announcement (PSA) Production Fund.

"The RM15 million allocation opens up avenues for emerging talents, expands international collaborations, provides space for veteran artistes to continue creating, and encourages the production of new content formats such as micro-dramas to meet digital market demands," Fahmi told reporters during the Anugerah Seri Angkasa (ASA) 2026 grand finale last night.
Local industry players can apply online through the Creative Industry Management and Monitoring System (SPPIK) at sppik.finas.my from the opening date.
Fahmi added that FINAS will share full guidelines, eligibility rules, and application steps on its official website and social media pages, urging local talent to seize the opportunity.
Turning to the prestigious broadcasting event, Fahmi stressed that the 37th edition of ASA was much more than a glamorous awards ceremony.
Instead, it serves as a meaningful way for the government to show its deep appreciation for everyone in the industry.

He noted that the recognition honours both on-screen personalities and the unsung heroes working behind the scenes, who all play a key role in sharing information, delivering quality entertainment, and boosting Malaysia's cultural identity and creative economy.

"On behalf of the government, Anugerah Seri Angkasa is not merely an awards ceremony, but a recognition of the contributions made by the entire broadcasting industry — covering those who work in front of the camera and behind the scenes in delivering information, producing quality entertainment, and strengthening Malaysia's identity and creative economy.

"The Madani government, through the Communications Ministry, will continue to strengthen the creative industry ecosystem through funding facilities, opportunities for fresh talent, and encouragement for the production of quality, competitive local content," he said.
At the ASA 2026 grand finale, held at the Putrajaya International Convention Centre, Datuk Rahim Razali received the prestigious Tokoh Seri Angkasa lifetime achievement award.
The top honours for best television drama went to Selampai Labung and Generasi: Perfect 10.
Azhan Rani and Noorkhiriah swept the main acting categories, while Bade Hj Azmi was named best director.

8e43f3fc69fa10b7: KADUNA: President Bola Tinubu formally launched his campaign for a second term on Saturday in the northern city of Kaduna, where he sought to convince voters that painful economic reforms are beginning to pay off despite a lingering cost-of-living crisis.

Tinubu, 74, faces a contest ahead of a Jan 16 election that is likely to be dominated by the economy and security. His main challengers include former vice-president Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, who finished second and third respectively in 2023.
By midday, thousands of supporters of the president's All Progressives Congress party had filled much of the 10,000-capacity Ranchers Bees Stadium, with more arriving as the rally got underway.
"Thank you for this massive showing up. It is a promise. Come 2027, January 16, you must go out massively and elect me again," Tinubu told the crowd.

Since taking office in 2023, Tinubu has scrapped fuel subsidies, devalued the naira and introduced other reforms credited with improving public finances, foreign reserves and investor sentiment. But the measures have also fuelled Nigeria's worst cost-of-living crisis in a generation.
Petrol prices rose to about 1,400 naira (US$1.05) a litre in Lagos and Abuja in September and as much as 1,500 naira in parts of northern Nigeria, adding to pressure on household budgets.
Tinubu dismissed opposition complaints about hunger and poverty, arguing that his rivals created those problems.
"They created the hunger. They created the poverty. We are trying to eradicate it."
Phrank Shaibu, a spokesman for the Atiku campaign, told Reuters the president was attempting to dodge responsibility.
"Mr President, blaming the opposition for hunger is either delusion or a staggering case of political amnesia," he said.

Security will provide another test. Nigeria continues to battle armed bandits and kidnappers in the northwest and a 17-year Islamist insurgency in the northeast, where militants have stepped up attacks on military positions.

Tinubu nevertheless enters the race with a formidable political machine. His camp says he has the backing of 32 of Nigeria's 36 state governors, potentially giving him an unprecedented organisational advantage, although past elections have shown governors cannot always deliver their states to presidential candidates.
His toughest electoral test could come in the north, where Atiku, a veteran northern politician with an established support base, will seek to erode the president's vote.

Tinubu has said he will not attend campaign rallies in all 36 states as he needs to remain focused on governing. The party's proposed timetable has him personally attending rallies in 12 states, culminating in a major closing rally in his home state of Lagos on Jan 9.

fbb6fd47c48582da: SOFIA: Bulgarians vote in presidential elections on Sunday as Russia's war in Ukraine spreads to the waters off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast.
Polls place acting president Iliana Iotova, 61, and former caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, as leaders in a race of 27 candidates.

While the presidency is largely ceremonial, Sunday's vote has taken on added significance after a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast that likely killed some two-dozen international seafarers.
The strikes, which sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine, prompted the government to seek allied assistance to bolster maritime security.
Bulgaria has stopped short of directly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks, but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said their outcome "benefits the Russian Federation".
Both leading presidential candidates condemned the strikes, but they differ over the broader war.

Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine. He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.
"I want Bulgaria to have a voice of its own in Europe. A reliable Nato ally that defends its interests through preparedness, strong diplomacy and a clear position," he said at a rally on Thursday.

Iotova, formerly vice-president, became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter the parliamentary race, which he won on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket. Radev supports Iotova and they both call for a diplomatic end to the war.
A victory for Iotova would make her Bulgaria's first elected female president.
"My opponents argue that there must be a war of attrition." she told a rally on Thursday. "The truth is, we are all the ones who are most exhausted."
Polls by Alpha Research give Iotova 41% of the vote and Gyurov 28%. If no candidate wins a majority, a runoff vote will be held on Nov 1.

d7ec5cf26e8bdc44: MANILA: Philippine police are investigating a laptop found alongside images of child abuse at the former home of Meghan Markle's estranged father, with "full results" expected in a week, the country's interior minister told AFP.
Thomas Markle, whose daughter is married to Britain's Prince Harry, had been living in Cebu in the Philippines until reportedly returning to the US earlier this year.

Philippine interior minister Jonvic Remulla told AFP the country planned to take "appropriate legal actions" against Markle -- who has denied all claims of alleged offending -- if sufficient evidence was found.

"The Philippine National Police (PNP), upon the reports of the son, inspected the former home of a certain Mr. Thomas Markle," Remulla said in a text message sent late Saturday. "Found were a trove of child pornography materials as well as a laptop."
"The laptop is currently going under forensic investigation and we will have the full results in one week," Remulla said.
"The PNP will coordinate with their counterparts to locate and take appropriate legal actions against Mr. Markle if found that there is sufficient evidence to charge him."
British tabloid the Sun first reported last week that Markle's son, Thomas Markle Jr, had discovered the child abuse images while going through boxes found in his father's former home.

On Friday, Meghan Markle said she was "deeply distressed" by accusations her father had possessed images of child abuse, adding she had blocked contact between him and her children over previous "troubling and disturbing" allegations.
After the reports, Meghan said that in 2018 she had seen a letter sent to London's Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection making similar accusations.
"It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father, and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," she said in a statement.
London's Metropolitan police said it had passed on the information to the royal couple but did not share it with other law enforcement agencies.
Meghan Markle and Prince Harry left Britain and quit royal duties in 2020 amid a bitter royal family feud.
They made an unexpected return with their children to live in the UK in August.
bcf005a71983164c: WASHINGTON, Oct 25 — The US Federal Reserve appears set to hold interest rates steady at its meeting next week, analysts say, despite stubbornly high inflation and with markets pricing in at least one rate hike before year-end.
The central bank’s Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will meet over two days, announcing its decision at 2:00 pm local time (18:00 GMT) on Wednesday.

The Fed has missed its long-term two-per cent target for inflation for more than five years, and at its last meeting in September the FOMC voted to raise the key federal funds rate for the first time in three years, lifting the target range to 3.75 per cent to 4.0 per cent.

The Fed’s meeting comes days ahead of key midterm elections in the United States on November 3, with the Democratic Party seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress from US President Donald Trump’s Republicans.

Trump frequently berated and criticised Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s predecessor Jerome Powell over interest rates – which he deems to be too high – but has so far refrained from targeting the man he appointed to replace him over the issue.

The Fed’s preferred gauge for inflation, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, hit a pandemic-era peak of 7.2 per cent in 2022, before a series of interest-rate hikes tamed it to around 2.2 per cent by late 2024.
Trump’s economic policies – including his upending of the global trade order using tariffs and his war on Iran – fuelled it once more, and it hit a three-year high of 3.9 per cent in May.
Since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February, global energy prices have skyrocketed, with Tehran’s retaliatory actions sharply curtailing oil and gas supplies through the Gulf.
Higher energy prices have begun to cascade through into other goods and services, fuelling inflation in the United States, with prices a key issue for voters as they head to the polls.
‘Based on the economics’
Loretta Mester, former regional head of the Cleveland Fed, told AFP that the timing of the meeting just days ahead of the election would not be a factor for policymakers.
“The Fed doesn’t take into account any kind of political issues in that FOMC room,” she said. “It really is based on the economics.”
Mester argued that the fundamentals call for continuing to raise interest rates.

“The data that’s come in continue to show a stable labour market and continue to show inflation above target,” she said, adding that there was no evidence that it was on a path downwards towards the target.
“The economics would suggest then you need to continue raising rates.”
Still, she thought that most policymakers seemed keen to avoid moving too quickly, and may hold rates at this meeting, waiting to tighten the screws until the following meeting in early December.
Wendy Edelberg, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, believes central bankers would rather not put themselves in the middle of the political debate ahead of the midterms.
“It’s unhelpful for everyone if the Fed gets wrapped up in all the political discourse right before an election,” she told AFP.
Edelberg said that “there wouldn’t be huge economic implications” if policymakers raised rates in December as opposed to October.
She saw such a decision less as a “nod to Trump” – who has aggressively demanded lower rates to spur economic activity – and more a way to avoid being the potential target of political barbs.

Since returning to power last year, the US president has waged an unprecedented assault on the Fed’s independence, launching a criminal probe against Powell and attempting to unseat Fed Governor Lisa Cook.
The probe against Powell was dropped to smooth the way for Warsh’s Senate confirmation, but the battle to fire Cook continues despite a Supreme Court decision nullifying an earlier attempt to do so.
Last week, Cook declined to attend a hearing in the White House’s probe into mortgage fraud allegations, which she denies. — AFP
e735de83078437b7: BUTTERWORTH, Oct 25 — Continuous heavy rain for several hours last night caused flash floods in several areas in Penang, inundating homes in Taman Cantek and Jalan Jelawat here.
In addition, several other areas in Bayan Lepas, Bayan Baru, Seberang Jaya, Ampang Jajar and Bukit Mertajam were also hit by flash floods, but no victims have been evacuated.
Penang Fire and Rescue Department assistant director of operations John Sagun Francis said it received an emergency call at 12.24am before dispatching personnel to the scenes.

“The flash floods in Taman Cantek affected 20 houses, with water levels estimated at 0.3 metres (one foot). The flooding was believed to have been caused by heavy rain and rising water levels in a nearby drain.
“We monitored the situation until it was under control and the water began to recede before ending the operation at 1.10am,” he said in a statement today.

He said flooding was also reported along Jalan Jelawat in Seberang Jaya as well as nearby residential areas, with water levels estimated at 0.3 metres due to continuous heavy rain and rising water levels in nearby drains. — Bernama
4f6ae21a771192e2: PETALING JAYA: Peguam mewakili keluarga Noorizwan Zulkefly yang meninggal dunia dalam tahanan polis mempertikaikan dapatan Bukit Aman bahawa Allahyarham tiada sebarang kecederaan dalaman.
Rania Aljunied, pengarah Lawyers for Liberty, dan Dina Zamri berkata dapatan itu bercanggah dengan hasil bedah siasat dijalankan pakar patologi dari Hospital Canselor Tuanku Muhriz UKM (HUKM).
Mereka berkata, laporan bedah siasat mendapati Noorizwan mengalami "pendarahan menyeluruh dalam otak" yang boleh menyebabkan kematian, selain pendarahan pada usus.

"Terdapat gambar bedah siasat jelas menunjukkan kecederaan itu. Dengan adanya bukti ini, bagaimana Bukit Aman boleh mengeluarkan kenyataan mendakwa si mati hanya mengalami kecederaan luaran dan tiada kecederaan dalaman?" kata mereka dalam kenyataan.

Mereka turut mempertikaikan kenyataan Bukit Aman berhubung punca kematian masih "menunggu analisis makmal" sedangkan pakar patologi telah menentukan lelaki berusia 42 tahun itu meninggal dunia disebabkan trauma akibat hentakan objek tumpul di kepala.
"Dapatan mengenai trauma objek tumpul ini tidak boleh diubah oleh analisis makmal terhadap sampel darah dan sampel lain yang belum selesai.
"Kenapa Bukit Aman berlengah-lengah dan memberi gambaran kepada orang ramai bahawa punca kematian belum dapat dipastikan? Perkara ini sama sekali tidak boleh diterima oleh pihak keluarga."
Mereka turut mempersoalkan kenapa polis masih mengklasifikasikan kes itu kematian mengejut dan bukannya kes bunuh sedangkan pelbagai bukti telah muncul.

Rania dan Dina menggesa Peguam Negara, Dusuki Mokhtar campur tangan serta mengarahkan kes itu disiasat sebagai kes bunuh, selain meminta sebuah pasukan khas ditubuhkan di Bukit Aman bagi mengambil alih siasatan berkenaan.
Mereka turut menggesa anggota polis disyaki terbabit kematian Noorizwan digantung tugas dan ditahan sementara menunggu siasatan selesai.
Noorizwan ditahan pada 19 Sept lalu bagi membantu siasatan berhubung kesalahan memiliki dadah, kecurian dan pecah rumah, sebelum ditempatkan di IPD Cheras.
Dia kemudian dikejarkan ke HUKM pada 30 Sept lalu, sebelum disahkan meninggal dunia keesokannya.
Semalam, Bukit Aman memaklumkan Noorizwan mengalami beberapa kecederaan pada bahagian luaran, tetapi tiada pendarahan dalaman dan punca kematiannya masih menunggu keputusan analisis makmal.
Perdana Menteri, Anwar Ibrahim kemudian mengarahkan ketua polis negara memastikan siasatan menyeluruh dan telus dijalankan ke atas kematian Noorizwan.
35ea072ba7ffb0ae: MELAKA, Oct 25 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim has urged the people of Melaka to reject politics of hatred based on race and religion, and instead strengthen unity as the foundation for national stability and progress.

Anwar, also Pakatan Harapan (PH) chairman, said the history of the Melaka Malay Sultanate and the nation’s independence struggle proves that momentous success comes through cooperation among various quarters, and not the struggle of a single group.
“I emphasise this repeatedly because some quarters attempt to distort history by claiming that this country can only be saved through the victory of a single race.
“If our ancestors succeeded in building the Melaka Malay Sultanate into a great empire, we can do the same through peace, unity among all quarters, and sound development strategies,” he said.
He said this when addressing the candidate announcement and launch of the Melaka PH election machinery for the Melaka state election at the Hang Jebat Stadium grounds here today.

Also present were DAP secretary-general Anthony Loke, Amanah president Datuk Seri Mohamad Sabu, PKR vice-president and PH election director Datuk Seri Amirudin Shari, and Melaka PH chairman Datuk Seri Adly Zahari.
Anwar said elections should serve as a platform to explain government achievements, policies, and future plans, rather than an arena to insult opponents or incite political hostility.
The government, he said, must be judged on its efforts to address bread-and-butter issues, including the cost of living, job opportunities, education, healthcare, and basic amenities.
Anwar stressed that strengthening unity does not mean sidelining the interests of the Malays and Bumiputeras, but that national development must be carried out through the cooperation of all races.

Melaka, he added, must continue to be developed through the active participation of the Malay, Chinese, and Indian communities to ensure the state prospers and secures a brighter future for the younger generation.

The Prime Minister cautioned that racial division could undermine the country’s drive to master emerging technologies, artificial intelligence (AI), and the digital economy, while stalling job creation and income growth.

Anwar said the government remains committed to rectifying administrative shortcomings and discharging the public trust responsibly, adding that peace and stability must be safeguarded for the nation’s well-being.

Touching on the Melaka state election, he urged voters to evaluate candidates based on their dedication and commitment to state development, while reminding the unveiled PH candidates to uphold the people’s trust and serve them diligently.
At the event, Anwar announced 21 candidates who will represent PH in the Melaka state election scheduled for Nov 14. — Bernama
5b617fee0c35136c: HEBRON: Israel said Sunday all land crossings with the West Bank will be closed on the day of next week's election, as it pledged a harder line on militancy after Palestinian gunmen killed two soldiers in the territory.

The announcement came a day after Israeli forces pushed into the occupied West Bank city of Hebron and displaced around 2,000 residents, with Defence Minister Israel Katz saying, "they will not be allowed to return... until we've finished dealing with all the Hamas issues in Hebron".
Hamas, while not claiming credit, hailed Friday's killings at a checkpoint near the Palestinian city, in which attackers shot dead two Israeli soldiers and wounded three more.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to exact a heavy price for the attack just days before polls and said he was planning an operation on a scale not seen since Israel first occupied the West Bank in 1967.

The Israeli army said that, from Sunday, Palestinians would "not be permitted to enter Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley for work", using terms many in Israel use to refer to the West Bank.

The army also said it would enforce "a ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers throughout Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley, including industrial zones, as well as the closure of all land crossings throughout Election Day" on October 27, it added.
Israel's longest serving prime minister Netanyahu is facing a tight race for a new term in Tuesday's polls, with his security-first reputation all but shattered by Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack.

The Palestinian Authority, the semi-autonomous body that governs parts of the West Bank in cooperation with Israel, called for international pressure on Israel to protect residents affected by the military operation.
The Israeli army said that over Friday and Saturday, it operated in 40 areas throughout the territory, with locals reporting that soldiers announced evacuations over loudspeakers late at night.
Israeli forces said they "apprehended approximately 40 suspects, including terrorists affiliated with the Hamas and Islamic Jihad terrorist organisations".

e6929fbc6e403d36: PERRY: US President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that Audi ​plans to build a US$4 billion assembly plant in Georgia that will produce 200,000 SUVs annually, as he seeks to convince Americans to back Republicans in the Nov 3 midterm elections.

Trump, who has pressured automakers to move ​production to the US and has raised tariffs on autos, steel, aluminum and ​parts, made the announcement at a rally in Perry, near Macon in central Georgia, where Volkswagen's (VW) premium subsidiary intends to build its first US assembly plant.
Last year, Trump's tariffs dealt Audi a €1.2-billion (US$1.4-billion) blow as it imports all its vehicles for the US market from Europe or Mexico.

Georgia has competitive election races for US Senate and governor. Trump is eager to make the case that his auto tariffs are helping the US economy. Critics say they have boosted vehicle prices and that the trade uncertainty has delayed some automaker investments.

"We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia," Audi CEO Gernot Doellner said at the event. "This is a this is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market."
Audi said the investment will create approximately 4,500 jobs. Construction is scheduled to begin next year, with production starting in the early 2030s, Audi said.
The plant is expected to assemble the Audi Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, a US official told Reuters.

Audi also plans to build 25,000 vehicles a year in neighboring South Carolina, the official said. Some of the vehicles, now built in Europe, would be exported, the official added. Those vehicles will be assembled at a US$2 billion plant of VW's off-road brand Scout Motors that is under construction in Blythewood, near the state capital, Columbia, the official said.

Trump has cut government incentives for electric vehicles, causing a significant reduction in US EV and battery production. US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year.
A gold Audi with manufacturer license plates was parked outside Trump's rally.

US Senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, said late on Saturday that "with this investment, Audi will build all of their SUVs exclusively in the US." He said the Audi plant "would never have happened without tariffs, without common sense regulations and without eliminating California’s ability to regulate fuel economy standards."
Audi sales have fallen for two consecutive years ​and slid 7% in the first half of 2026 as fierce competition ⁠in China and US tariffs hit demand. Audi's US sales are down 16% this year.
Audi's Neckarsulm plant in southwest Germany is one of four German Volkswagen plants facing possible closure after 2030.

In July, Japan's Toyota said it would spend US$3.6 billion to build a 232,000-square-metre truck assembly line on its San Antonio, Texas, manufacturing campus and shift some truck production to the US from Mexico. The Japanese automaker said the expansion would be completed by 2030, creating 2,000 jobs.

Honda Motor is considering building a US assembly plant but has warned it may not unless the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement on trade is extended. South Korea's Hyundai said last year that if it had certainty about USMCA, it "would immediately unlock over US$20 billion in new American investments."

0ba1034398826635: PETALING JAYA: Lawyers acting for the family of the late Noorizwan Zulkefly, who died under police detention, have disputed Bukit Aman's findings that the deceased did not suffer any internal injury.
Rania Aljunied, a Lawyers for Liberty director, and Dina Zamri said this contradicted the findings of an autopsy conducted by a Hospital Canselor Tuanku Muhriz UKM (HUKM) pathologist.

"Why then is Bukit Aman dragging its feet and insinuating to the public that the cause of death is still uncertain? This is entirely unacceptable to the family."
They also questioned why the police are still classifying the case as sudden death rather than a murder, given the evidence that has surfaced.
Rania and Dina urged Attorney-General Dusuki Mokhtar to step in and order the case to be probed as a murder, and for a special team in Bukit Aman to take over the probe.
They also called for the policemen suspected to have been involved in Noorizwan's death to be suspended and detained pending investigations.
Noorizwan was arrested on Sept 19 in connection with an investigation into drug possession, theft, and a break-in, and held at the Cheras police headquarters.
He was rushed to HUKM on Sept 30 and pronounced dead the following day.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has ordered the inspector-general of police to ensure a thorough and transparent investigation into Noorizwan's death.
2d634e807c3a6210: OCTOBER 25 — When global oil markets become volatile, Malaysian consumers face a different reality at the petrol station. For eligible recipients under the Budi Madani RON95 (BUDI95) programme, RON95 petrol remains priced at RM1.99 per litre, compared with the unsubsidised price of RM4.32 per litre for the period from October 22 to 28, 2026.

That difference is more than a figure displayed at the pump. It raises a broader question about consumer welfare: how does fuel price protection help households manage everyday expenses, and how can that support remain fair and financially sustainable?
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Yesterday, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim announced a temporary adjustment to the quota for the Budi Madani RON95 (BUDI95) programme from 300 litres to 200 litres per month, effective April 1. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin
More than a price at the pump

For many Malaysians, petrol is an essential household expense. It enables people to commute to work, take children to school, attend medical appointments and meet other daily responsibilities. For households that depend on private vehicles, a predictable fuel price can make budgeting easier and reduce uncertainty when planning other essential spending.

From a consumer behaviour perspective, this predictability matters. When people have a clearer idea of a recurring expense, they can make more informed decisions about how to allocate limited household income. A subsidy can therefore provide practical relief, particularly where affordable and reliable public transport is not readily available.

However, a stable petrol price should not be mistaken for overall price stability. The prices of food, housing and other necessities are shaped by many factors, including labour costs, exchange rates, logistics, supply conditions and competition. Fuel is one part of the cost-of-living picture, not its only driver.
Balancing consumer protection and public spending

Fuel subsidies can cushion eligible consumers from some of the immediate effects of changes in international energy markets. But this protection comes at a public cost. For the week of October 22 to 28, the difference between the unsubsidised RON95 price and the BUDI95 price is RM2.33 per litre. This illustrates the scale of support provided at the point of purchase, while also highlighting the importance of responsible public spending.

The policy challenge is not simply to decide whether subsidies are good or bad. It is to consider who benefits, whether assistance reaches those who need it, and how the government can sustain support alongside other public priorities such as healthcare, education and public transport.

Targeted assistance can help focus public resources on eligible consumers, but its effectiveness depends on clear rules, accessible implementation and transparent communication. People need to understand who qualifies, what limits apply and how the policy works. Support should also be reviewed with attention to households whose circumstances make them particularly vulnerable to increases in living costs.
Looking beyond fuel prices

Fuel subsidies are only one element of consumer protection. Businesses should provide clear and fair pricing, while policymakers should monitor market conditions and communicate changes in a way that consumers can understand. It is important not to assume that every increase in the price of fuel must lead directly to an increase in the price of every good or service. The relationship depends on the role of fuel in production and distribution, as well as on other market conditions.

Over the longer term, better public transport and greater energy efficiency can give households more choices and reduce dependence on fuel-intensive travel. These measures should complement immediate assistance, rather than leave individuals to bear the burden of adjustment on their own.
Measuring the real value of subsidies

The value of Malaysia’s fuel subsidy should not be measured solely by the price consumers pay per litre. It should also be assessed through household affordability, the fairness of assistance, the clarity of its delivery and the responsible use of public funds.

A subsidised price can offer meaningful protection in an uncertain energy market. The task is to ensure that this protection remains well targeted, transparent and sustainable. Regular evaluation can help policymakers understand whether assistance is easing pressure on household budgets and whether its benefits are reaching the people it is intended to support.

Ultimately, fuel subsidies are not merely about the price of petrol. They are part of a wider conversation about consumer welfare, economic resilience and the relationship between public policy and everyday life. The real value of a subsidy lies not only in what consumers save today, but also in whether the policy can continue to support households fairly and responsibly over time.

*Nurul Fardini Zakaria is a Senior Lecturer in Marketing at the School of Business Management, Universiti Utara Malaysia (UUM), with expertise in consumer behaviour, digital marketing, sustainable consumption and consumer welfare.
** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
e80ad09da63cd16b: SINGAPORE, Oct 25 — A sudden reduction in piped natural gas supplies from Indonesia will account for less than 2 per cent of Singapore's total daily gas demand, the Energy Market Authority (EMA) confirmed, adding that alternative liquefied natural gas (LNG) reserves and contingency protocols will prevent any disruption to the power grid.
The market regulator was responding to announcements from Jakarta that Indonesia would scale back deliveries through two subsea pipelines feeding the island nation.

Indonesian upstream regulator SKK Migas chief Djoko Siswanto told local media that Jakarta would reduce natural gas exports to Singapore by 31 billion British thermal units per day (BBTUD) starting Oct 24.

However, the EMA clarified that data from Singapore's licensed gas importers points to a smaller curtailment of 17 BBTUD spread over 18 days, a fraction of the republic's daily consumption exceeding 1,000 BBTUD, The Straits Times reported.

“EMA understands that our importers will pursue all relevant recourse in their contracts for the gas supply disruption,” the spokesman added, emphasizing that the city-state regularly absorbs operational fluctuations between 20 and 100 BBTUD during routine maintenance cycles without incident.

Singapore generates roughly 95 per cent of its electricity from natural gas, relying on pipeline links from Malaysia and Indonesia alongside globally sourced LNG cargoes. The EMA noted that Singapore GasCo, the nation's central gas procurement entity, stands operationally primed to import supplemental shipments at short notice.
“Besides Indonesia, Singapore imports natural gas from other sources around the world.
“Power generation companies are further required to maintain sufficient fuel reserves for power generation, including diesel reserves.”

On the corporate front, Temasek-owned Gas Supply acknowledged that deliveries to local industrial clients faced “temporary reductions” from its Indonesian upstream counterpart, confirming direct discussions to cushion the operational shortfall.
“(The company) continues to engage closely with our upstream supplier to manage the situation,” the importer stated.

The pipeline curtailment follows pointed rhetoric from Indonesian Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Bahlil Lahadalia, who warned on Oct 22 that Jakarta could restrict energy shipments to nations that fail to demonstrate mutual respect.

Indonesian media have characterised the cuts, which involve 15 BBTUD from the Natuna offshore corridor and 16 BBTUD from the Jambi Merang field in Sumatra, as part of President Prabowo Subianto's drive to prioritise domestic energy security.
Sumatran gas flows directly to Gas Supply, while Natuna offshore gas feeds into Sembcorp Gas receiving terminals under long-term sales agreements scheduled to run until 2028.

Energy market economists noted that while turning to spot LNG can occasionally elevate marginal procurement costs, the modest scale of the cut means consumer electricity tariffs will absorb minimal impact.

Solar Energy Research Institute of Singapore chief executive Subodh Mhaisalkar noted that LNG acts as a critical strategic shock absorber, observing that the shortfall represents a “small portion” of daily generation needs.

Independent energy economist David Broadstock described the sudden reduction as a “surprising event” in Singapore's supply chain, noting that the timing coincides with the eve of Singapore International Energy Week and ongoing bilateral friction over transboundary haze enforcement.
“There is a question mark over whether there is a political element tied to this action, potentially making it a reaction to the haze issue.
“I wouldn’t say for sure that it is a definitive driving factor, but it certainly cannot be ruled out.”

Analysts highlighted that with LNG currently accounting for roughly 60 per cent of Singapore's gas mix, the pipeline row will likely accelerate Singapore's push toward regional electricity grid interconnectors and renewable investments.
eecca74aa31b0575: PETALING JAYA: The Sultan of Selangor, Sultan Sharafuddin Idris Shah, says he is fed up with excessive and unproductive politicking.
“Like the rakyat, I am also fed up,” he said in a special interview with Bernama, marking his 25 years on the Selangor throne.
He urged politicians in the state to focus on serving the people, promoting economic growth and preserving unity to maintain the state's leading position in the country.
The sultan said there was no place for politics that exploited race and religion or dragged the royalty into political disputes.

“Selangor’s strength has always been its people. We are blessed with a society made up of different races, religions and cultures that have lived, worked and prospered together for generations,” he said.
Sultan Sharafuddin acknowledged that politicians had every right to debate policies, offer different ideas and compete for public support.
“However, politics should never come at the expense of racial harmony or religious understanding.”
The sultan also reminded politicians to avoid sensitive remarks that could hurt the feelings of others. “Don't be a hero or a 'stirrer'. Think before you speak and always be mindful.”
He said Selangor, like Malaysia, had been built on compromise, mutual respect and a willingness to appreciate differences while pursuing common goals.
With social media enabling messages to reach millions within minutes, he warned that irresponsible statements could have serious consequences.
“A single irresponsible statement can easily inflame emotions, deepen mistrust and create unnecessary tension among communities.

“This is why public figures must exercise wisdom, restraint and a deep sense of responsibility. Leadership is measured not only by what one says but also by the consequences those words have on society.”
Sultan Sharafuddin said everyone stood to lose when race and religion were repeatedly used to divide communities or create fear and suspicion.
The ruler also attributed Selangor's success to its diversity, stability and inclusiveness.
“Investors come here because they see a state that is peaceful and forward-looking. Our young people want opportunities, quality education, good jobs, affordable housing and a better future.
“My advice to all political leaders, regardless of party, is simple: place the interests of the people above political interests.

“Uphold the Federal Constitution, respect the position of Islam as the religion of the federation while safeguarding the rights of other religions to be practised in peace and harmony, and preserve the spirit of moderation that has long been the foundation of Selangor.”
He expressed disappointment over the mismanagement of Tabung Haji, stressing that funds entrusted for religious purposes must be managed with accountability and responsibility.
Asked what advice he would offer the next generation of rulers and leaders, he said leadership must always be regarded as a trust.
“Listen before deciding, remain humble regardless of success, uphold the Constitution faithfully and never lose sight of the people whom you are called to serve.

“A ruler must be prepared to listen more than he speaks, to seek counsel from those with knowledge and experience, and to make decisions guided not by personal interest but by what is best for the state and its people.
“A sultan must be a symbol of unity for all, treating every citizen with compassion, dignity and impartiality.
“Always remain humble in your behaviour, choice of words and actions,” he advised, adding that no ruler could succeed alone.

f4aa9945c30bcf1a: KUALA LUMPUR: Selepas lebih tiga dekad menghasilkan lagu popular untuk penyanyi tempatan, Aubrey Suwito akhirnya diraikan sebagai figura utama persembahan Orkestra Simfoni Kebangsaan (OSK).

Komposer berusia 60 tahun itu mencipta sejarah sebagai komposer tempatan pertama menerima penghormatan tersebut menerusi konsert OSK with Aubrey Suwito: Pop Meets Symphony di Panggung Sari, Istana Budaya, pada 2 dan 3 Okt lalu.
Sebanyak 16 karya ciptaannya termasuk Gemilang, Seribu Impian, Memori Tercipta, Gemuruh dan Lebih Indah, dipersembahkan semula dalam susunan muzik simfoni.

Aubrey berkata, pada mulanya sukar mempercayai pemilihan itu, namun menganggapnya sebagai pengiktirafan bukan sahaja kepada dirinya, malah komposer dan tenaga kreatif yang selama ini bekerja di belakang tabir.
“Soalan pertama saya, betul ke?” katanya kepada FMT.

Katanya, penghormatan itu lebih bermakna kerana bukan sahaja mengangkat penyanyi yang berada di hadapan pentas, malah memberi pengiktirafan kepada komposer serta tenaga kreatif yang selama ini bekerja di belakang tabir.
“Saya rasa bangga kerana bukan saja orang di hadapan pentas diraikan, tetapi juga orang belakang tabir,” katanya.

“Penghormatan ini bukan sekadar meraikan perjalanan seni saya, malah simbol penghargaan kepada ramai komposer, penggubah muzik dan penerbit yang selama ini menyumbang kepada industri tanpa banyak menerima sorotan,” katanya.

Penerima 26 Anugerah Industri Muzik (AIM) itu berkata, susunan muzik untuk konsert berkenaan mengambil masa hampir tiga bulan untuk disiapkan, dengan setiap lagu memerlukan empat hingga enam hari kerja.
Katanya, pengalaman dan latihan berterusan penting dalam membentuk kemahiran seseorang pemuzik, sama seperti juruterbang yang perlu mengumpul ribuan jam penerbangan.
Aubrey yang pernah bekerjasama dengan Siti Nurhaliza, David Foster dan Brian McKnight serta merupakan graduan Berklee College of Music, kini turut berminat meneroka muzik tradisional.
Konsert itu turut memperkenalkan lagu baharunya, Jodoh, nyanyian Shiha Zikir dipersembahkan buat kali pertama kepada penonton.
“Harapan saya, muzik pop, simfoni dan tradisional tidak lagi dilihat berasingan, tetapi berkembang sebagai satu landskap muzik yang saling melengkapi,” katanya.
Sementara itu, pengarah persembahan Mohd Fairuz Tauhid atau Cikgu Fee berkata konsert tersebut memberinya peluang mengenali sisi Aubrey yang selama ini hanya dikenali menerusi karya ciptaannya.
Katanya, Aubrey bukan sahaja komposer berpengalaman malah tidak lokek berkongsi idea sepanjang sesi perbincangan serta latihan.

“Cabaran terbesar bukanlah menghasilkan sebuah persembahan simfoni, sebaliknya mencari keseimbangan antara muzik pop yang dekat dengan masyarakat dan orkestra yang sering dianggap eksklusif,” katanya yang kali pertama bekerjasama dengan OSK menerusi persembahan itu.
Penyanyi Syamel dan Ernie Zakri pula menyifatkan pemilihan Aubrey sebagai pengiktirafan yang wajar terhadap sumbangannya kepada industri muzik tempatan.
Bagi Shiha, kepercayaan diberikan untuk menyampaikan lagu baharu itu bukan sekadar penampilan khas malah penghormatan besar apabila dipilih oleh komposer tersohor.
“Saya memang berharap sangat dapat bekerjasama dengan Aubrey kerana setiap lagu dihasilkannya ada semangat dan jiwa tersendiri,” katanya.
cc25045ec6545ebf: KUALA LUMPUR: For more than three decades, Aubrey Suwito has been the name behind some of Malaysia's best music - writing, arranging and producing songs that became part of the soundtrack of Malaysian pop.

This month, the spotlight finally turned his way. The 60-year-old became the first local composer to be honoured with his own National Symphony Orchestra concert through “NSO with Aubrey Suwito: Pop Meets Symphony”, held at Panggung Sari, Istana Budaya, on Oct 2 and 3.

Sixteen of his compositions, including “Gemilang”, “Seribu Impian”, “Memori Tercipta”, “Gemuruh” and “Lebih Indah”, were reimagined with symphonic arrangements, giving familiar songs a new scale and sweep.
For Aubrey, being chosen still feels like a dream. “My first question was, ‘Is this for real?’” he told FMT.
What moved him most, he said, was not simply being feted as an individual, but seeing recognition extended to the people whose work so often happens away from the stage.
“I feel proud because it’s not only the people in front of the stage who are being celebrated, but also those behind the scenes,” he said.

“This honour is not just a celebration of my artistic journey, but also a symbol of appreciation for the many composers, arrangers and producers who have contributed to the industry without receiving much attention.”

Aubrey knows that world well. A recipient of 26 Anugerah Industri Muzik (AIM) awards, he has worked with artistes including Siti Nurhaliza, David Foster and Brian McKnight. His training at Berklee College of Music helped shape a career built as much on craft as instinct.
Preparing for the concert itself was no small undertaking. Aubrey said the symphonic arrangements took almost three months to complete, with each song requiring between four and six days of work.

To him, that level of discipline is simply part of being a musician. He likened it to a pilot accumulating thousands of flight hours: experience and constant practice, he said, are what sharpen instinct and confidence over time.
The concert also gave audiences something entirely new: “Jodoh”, Aubrey’s latest composition, performed publicly for the first time by Shiha Zikir.

Even after decades in pop, Aubrey remains curious about where music can take him next. He is now especially interested in exploring traditional sounds and finding ways for different musical worlds to meet.
“My hope is that pop, symphonic and traditional music will no longer be seen as separate, but will develop as one musical landscape that complements itself,” he said.

That spirit of openness shaped the production itself. Performance director Fairuz Tauhid, better known as Cikgu Fee, said working on the concert allowed him to discover a side of Aubrey he had previously known mainly through his compositions.
He described Aubrey as generous with ideas throughout rehearsals and discussions, despite his decades of experience.

“The biggest challenge was not producing a symphonic performance, but finding the balance between pop music, which is close to the public, and orchestral music, which is often seen as exclusive,” said Fairuz, who was working with the NSO for the first time.
For singers Syamel and Ernie Zakri, the concert was a fitting tribute to someone whose contribution to Malaysian music has long been heard, even if he has not always been seen.
Shiha felt much the same way. Being entrusted with “Jodoh”, she said, was more than simply another performance - it was a chance to work directly with a composer she had long admired.
“I really hoped I would get the chance to work with Aubrey because every song he creates has spirit and soul,” she said.

68b8fa9b95dac59e: From Wan Agyl Wan Hassan
Malaysia’s debate over minimum e-hailing fares is about more than the price of a ride.
This raises a fundamental question: how do we protect drivers’ livelihoods without making everyday mobility more expensive for the public?
E-hailing has changed how Malaysians travel. It offers convenience, flexible earning opportunities and an important transport option in areas where conventional public transport remains inadequate.
For some commuters, it also provides the crucial connection between home and the nearest rail station.
Yet behind that convenience is an economic imbalance that deserves attention.

Drivers bear much of the cost of providing the service. Fuel, maintenance, insurance, financing and vehicle depreciation come out of their pockets. They also absorb the cost of travelling to pick-up points, returning without passengers and waiting between bookings.
These are legitimate concerns. However, increasing the minimum passenger fare does not necessarily resolve them.
What passengers pay and what drivers actually earn are not the same thing.
Consider two drivers. One completes a RM12 journey but waits another 45 minutes for the next booking.
Another completes two RM8 journeys over a similar period with little waiting time.
Depending on distance and operating expenses, the second driver could earn more despite charging less per trip.

This illustrates why driver welfare cannot be measured by individual fares alone. What matters is how much a driver retains after expenses and how many productive hours they achieve throughout the working day.
Our research into Malaysia’s e-hailing economy highlights the financial pressures faced by drivers.
Based on our operating-cost model, running a Perodua Bezza for e-hailing services costs approximately RM0.40 per kilometre, including fuel, maintenance, insurance and vehicle depreciation.
While this is an indicative estimate rather than an industry-wide benchmark, our findings highlight an important reality: drivers continue to incur costs even when they are not carrying passengers.
Travelling to pick-up points, repositioning between bookings and waiting for the next journey all affect their actual take-home earnings.
This is why proposals for a minimum base fare, distance tariff and time-based compensation require careful examination.

A five-kilometre journey through Kuala Lumpur during evening congestion is very different from a similar journey on a free-flowing suburban road. The distance may be identical, but the time commitment and opportunity to secure subsequent bookings are not.
Conditions also differ outside major cities, where drivers may face longer waiting periods and fewer passengers.
A uniform national fare formula could therefore benefit some drivers while disadvantaging others.
Without reliable information on actual operating costs, trip demand and driver utilisation, setting a statutory rate risks creating new problems even as it attempts to solve existing ones.
There is also the passenger to consider.

For many Malaysians, e-hailing is not a luxury. It is a practical transport option, particularly where buses are infrequent, rail stations are difficult to reach or travelling without a private vehicle is inconvenient.
In Greater Kuala Lumpur, some commuters depend on e-hailing for short journeys to MRT and LRT stations.
If that connection becomes disproportionately expensive, the entire public transport journey becomes less attractive.
Some may return to driving or riding motorcycles. Others may simply travel less.
Neither outcome should be dismissed when Malaysia is investing heavily in improving public transport accessibility.
However, affordable feeder services should not come at the expense of drivers.
If the government wants to encourage first- and last-mile connectivity, targeted subsidies, integrated ticketing and demand-responsive transit should be considered.
Drivers should not be expected to absorb the cost of achieving national public transport objectives.
This brings us to the more important regulatory question: should Malaysia focus on setting minimum passenger fares or protecting minimum driver earnings?

The Gig Workers Act 2025 provides an opportunity to examine this distinction. Through the Gig Workers’ Consultative Council, Malaysia now has a statutory mechanism for considering minimum earnings rates and formulas appropriate to different categories of gig work.

Rather than immediately imposing a uniform passenger fare floor, policymakers should examine whether minimum driver remuneration, supported by reasonable expense recovery, would offer more direct protection.

Such an approach must also address unpaid working time such as dead mileage. Protecting earnings only while a passenger is onboard may still leave drivers exposed to long periods of uncompensated waiting.

Platform accountability is equally important. Malaysia already has commission ceilings for e-hailing services, but regulators must ensure that deductions are transparent, existing requirements are enforced and drivers understand how their earnings are calculated.
Reducing commission ceilings may appear attractive, but its effects on platform viability, incentives, competition and passenger prices must also be assessed.

The wider institutional framework deserves attention. Transport regulation, worker protection and competition oversight involve different authorities. Whether Malaysia strengthens existing institutions or establishes additional regulatory arrangements, responsibilities must be clear and enforcement effective.
Creating another regulatory body will not automatically improve driver earnings if the underlying economic problems remain unresolved.

Before introducing binding fare formulas, Malaysia needs a credible assessment of driver operating costs, actual take-home earnings, unpaid mileage, working hours, platform deductions and passenger affordability.
The findings should guide regulation, not the other way around.

Drivers deserve fair remuneration for their time, effort and investment. Passengers deserve affordable and reliable mobility. Platforms need sustainable commercial conditions, while regulators must protect the wider public interest.
These objectives need not conflict, but achieving them requires evidence rather than assumptions.

Malaysia should not confuse higher fares with better livelihoods. The true measure of successful e-hailing regulation is whether drivers earn a reasonable return, passengers can still afford to travel and the transport system continues to serve both.
That is the equilibrium worth pursuing.
Wan Agyl Wan Hassan is the founder and senior adviser to MY Mobility Vision, a transport think tank.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

50156b4defde56fe: Kita kini berdepan dengan moraliti baharu. Biasanya seseorang yang didapati bersalah atau kalah saman maka pihak itu dikatakan kalah dan tidak berada dalam kebenaran moral. Namun demikian, perkara terbalik kini mungkin terjadi apabila pihak kalah dilihat sebagai mangsa penghakiman dan ia juga dilihat sebagai pejuang kaum atau agama. Saya akan membentangkan dua kajian kes dalam hal ini.

Kajian kes pertama adalah kes saman Teresa Kok daripada DAP ke atas Dr Akmal Saleh daripada Umno yang berakhir dengan kemenangan mahkamah kepada Kok dengan perintah supaya Akmal membayar RM300,000. Manakala kes kedua adalah saman Kok, Lim Kit Siang dan Lim Guan Eng ke atas Siti Mastura Muhammad daripada PAS yang berakhir dengan perintah mahkamah supaya wakil rakyat PAS itu membayar RM850,000. Jelas dalam satu perspektif DAP menang 2-0 dan PAS serta Umno tewas teruk. Namun, bagaimana pula perspektif politik? Ini yang menarik, tuan-tuan. Dalam bacaan saya DAP kalah 0-2 manakala PAS menang 1-0 dan Umno menang 1-0. Pelik kan? Tak juga, ia adalah politik ala Melayu.

Dalam kes pertama, Akmal didapati bersalah menghina Kok sehingga menyifatkan beliau sebagai musuh Islam. Kita semua dengan jelas dapat membaca sendiri kata-kata kasar Akmal dengan penggunaan ‘nyonya tua’ serta nak bagi cop halal pada dahinya. Hakim mahkamah telah menyimpulkan Akmal bertindak di luar daripada adab perbezaan pendapat dan debat politik kepada sesuatu yang membahayakan masyarakat, sefaham saya. Maka, Akmal diperintahkan membayar Kok RM300,000.

Maka, timbullah keesokannya gambar Akmal dengan nada sedih duduk termenung depan kolam ikan tilapianya sambil mengungkap untuk menjual motosikal dan ikannya melalui lelongan supaya dapat membayar Kok. Diberitakan hanya beberapa jam sahaja beliau dapat mengutip lebih RM40,000 ke dalam akaun peribadinya. Namun demikian, beliau berkeras tidak mahu orang menderma dan masih mahu menjalankan lelongannya seperti dibuat oleh sahabat Umno lain, Jamal Yunos. Kok nampaknya meraih banyak kekayaan dengan samannya yang lumayan. Jadi, soalannya bagaimana pula dikatakan DAP kalah politik dan Umno menang pula dalam hal ini? Sabar, tuan-tuan, kita ulas kes kedua pula.

Dalam kajian kes kedua, kita berdepan dengan kenyataan Mastura yang memfitnah Guan Eng dan Kit Siang sebagai sepupu kepada Lee Kuan Yew. Walaupun jelas pangkal nama Lim dan Lee berbeza entah macam mana seorang yang bergelar PhD tidak faham akan nama orang Cina. Bila dituduh memfitnah, Mastura mengemukakan ‘bukti’ daripada buku kempen Barisan Nasional. Tetapi, oleh kerana buku itu tiada nama penulis maka sukar untuk dibawa bukti kerana tiada badan yang nak menjawab. Mastura sepatutnya tidak meletakkan kredibiliti yang tinggi kepada suatu sumber yang memang tugasnya berperang politik. Dalam peperangan, anything goes asalkan menang. Maka, menanglah orang DAP dan Mastura berdepan pembayaran yang bukan kepalang sedikit; hampir RM1 juta. Nasib baik, PAS menggerakkan partinya dengan membuat gerakan ‘derma jihad’ pada keseluruhan jentera. Surat yang ditulis seperti tidak mengaku kesalahan tetapi membuat episod itu sebagai ‘perjuangan Islam’. Maka, dalam kurang lebih seminggu, wang sejumlah banyak itu dapat dikutip dan terus diserahkan kepada pihak peguam. Memang PAS cukup hebat dan saya pun mengagumi parti tersebut yang berjaya mengutip dengan pantas. Hari ini, dah lebih satu bulan, wang RM50 juta belum siap Umno kutip lagi, dan entah bila Najib Razak dapat pulang ke pangkuan keluarga. Jadi, soalannya bagaimana pula dikatakan yang DAP kalah politik dan PAS menang pula?

Begini, saya lihat moral orang Islam dan Melayu daripada kajian kes kedua-duanya. Dalam kes Akmal, penyokong Umno dan Akmal yang saya anggap semuanya Melayu tidak mempunyai pandangan bahawa ada kesalahan pun apabila Akmal bercakap kasar dan membuatkan Kok seperti seorang musuh Islam. Ramai orang Melayu sudah selesa dengan naratif DAP musuh Melayu dan Islam, jadi tidaklah surprise, yang penyokong Akmal masih menganggap Akmal sebagai the hero dan Kok sebagai the villain. Dunia dah terbalik agaknya di mana yang mengasari dianggap betul dan yang dikasari dianggap tidak betul. Jadi, apabila lelongan atau derma kilat kepada Akmal mungkin terkutip dalam kurang lebih seminggu, kita akan mendapat satu moraliti politik yang baharu bahawa untuk berjuang kita kena kasar dan menuduh sebarang apa pun as long as it works. Itu nampaknya adab baharu dalam politik Melayu. Jadi, sah Akmal lagi popular dan Kok serta DAP lagi lebih dibenci Melayu. So, Akmal menang, Kok kalah dalam politik 'Malaysia boleh'.

Dalam kajian kes kedua, terdapat moral lebih berat lagi yang diterima pakai oleh orang Melayu. Dengan bukti cepatnya koleksi ‘derma jihad’ maka jihad Islam dah masuk menyokong fitnah yang disahkan pengadilan mahkamah dan pengadilan umum. Tetapi, oleh kerana sayangnya Melayu kepada agama Islam dan parti yang menempik sebagai pejuang nombor wahid Islam maka fitnah kepada orang bukan Islam seperti macam tak ada nilai langsung dari aspek dosa dan pahala. Malah, silap hari bulan membantu mangsa saman DAP mungkin dianggap mendapat pahala dengan menderma wang ringgit yang sepatutnya boleh diberi makan anak beranak atau fakir miskin. Ini bukan sahaja suatu evolusi moral Melayu tetapi ia melangkaui kepada nilai Islam; menyokong fitnah untuk membantu perjuangan Islam. Oleh yang demikian saya membuat deklarasi bahawa PAS-Mastura menang dan DAP bertiga kalah dalam politik ala Islam di Malaysia.

Paling menarik juga bagi saya, kes Jamal tidak mendapat bantuan daripada penyokong Umno maka beliau kekal tewas mahkamah dan tewas politik Melayu sebab tiada derma kilat untuknya. Nampaknya, setelah 40 tahun saya mengikuti politik Islam di Malaysia, baru kini saya dapat lihat perkembangan moral ‘Islam’ baharu didikan dua parti besar Melayu. Syabaslah saya ucapkan.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
52bd68910fc3a807: Sabah and Sarawak have long been touted as examples of what Malaysian unity is supposed to look like. We are told that in these two states, people of various faiths and races live together effortlessly.
Apparently, everyone in East Malaysia celebrates each other’s festivals as a family. There are no reservations among those of different faiths or suspicions that one group is out to get another.
I am told that in Sabah and Sarawak, people of different races even sit at the same table in a coffeeshop.
This scenario harkens back to a time when Malay Muslims in the peninsula were not as conservative as they are nowadays — a time when they were more relaxed and would mix well with other Malaysians.
That is in stark contrast to the Taliban-like mentality we encounter these days.
Unfortunately, it seems religious and racial parochialism may have now arrived on Sabah and Sarawak’s shores.
A Sarawakian MP’s concern about primary schoolers not wanting to sit next to pork-consuming or crucifix-wearing classmates is the most damning proof that conservatism has set foot in East Malaysia.
In truth, religious conservatism did not appear in East Malaysia overnight.

I do recall the controversy over plans to construct a statue of Mazu, the Chinese goddess of the sea, which was abandoned in 2006 following objections by the Muslim community on the grounds that the site was too near the town mosque.
In 2024, a petrol bomb was thrown at a KK Mart outlet in Kuching in the wake of the “Allah” socks controversy.
And just last month, there was an uproar over a concert by US gospel singer Israel Houghton, with his name and stance on Israel triggering sensitivities within the community.
How did this come to be? A change in demographics?

Sure, Sabah and Sarawak’s Malay population may have increased. Even so, the community's attitude towards religion remains considerably more tolerant than that of its counterparts in Peninsular Malaysia.
But I blame the rapid spread of technology, especially the internet and social media.
Extremist views and fiery rhetoric can now be accessed around the clock, fuelling hatred and poisoning the younger generation.
Strict immigration controls are powerless against the digital penetration of extremist ideologies and divisive rhetoric.
Sabah and Sarawak risk losing their status as the last bastion of the Malaysian way of life envisioned by our forefathers.

At the risk of being ridiculed for saying so, I fear that within the next decade the two states could become just as consumed by racial and religious rhetoric as parts of Peninsular Malaysia are today.
But, despite my pessimistic outlook, all is not lost, yet.
The two East Malaysia states must look into retraining teachers of religion and history — two subjects that must integrate aspects of nation building.
History must be taught in a more inclusive manner: the contributions of every race and tribe should be acknowledged when speaking about the state and country’s development.
After all, there is a wealth of evidence to show how all races and faiths have contributed to Malaysia’s growth.
It is just a matter of having these contributions documented, preferably by a group of honest Malaysians who believe in the idea of a true Malaysia for all.
There are also ways to weave the values Islam teaches into the Rukun Negara while educating Muslims on how to coexist in a plural society.
Sabah and Sarawak have shown their autonomous streak in recognising the Unified Examination Certificate. Sarawak uses English alongside Bahasa Malaysia for official purposes.
The two states should likewise use their autonomy to counter the growing influence of narrow and divisive worldviews.
Sabah and Sarawak stand as the final bastion of the Malaysian ideal envisioned by our forefathers, one built on mutual respect, coexistence and shared progress.
Sadly, Peninsular Malaysia is a lost cause since the malady it suffers from cannot be treated without severe backlash.
But if Sabah and Sarawak dilly-dally on this issue, even they will not escape the threats that race and religious extremism can bring.
And, this time, we won’t be able to pin the blame on politicians.
